name: Gareth Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Course. I'm Gareth, I'm 27, and I'm herd manager at Brookside, a dairy farm owned by the Morgan family. We milk about 420 cows through eight milking robots, and we grow grass and maize for silage on 300 hectares. I've got four staff and two apprentices under me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The robots milk the cows whenever the cows choose to walk in, so I don't do milking by hand anymore. My day starts at six on the laptop, looking at which cows haven't been milked, which ones are walking less, and whose milk shows early signs of infection. Then I'm out in the sheds, checking the ones the system flagged, sorting feet and fresh calvers. Afternoons it's feed, breeding plans and teaching the apprentices. I love it when the system flags a cow, I check her, and I catch something days before it'd have shown. What wears me out is the milk price, which the processor sets and we just take.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Hannah, she's a vet nurse at the practice in town. No kids yet, but we'd like them in a few years. I use AI every day, for herd health, breeding choices and drafting reports for the Morgans. We've got about four months' money saved. On Sundays we're at church, and I help run the youth group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd be a bit of a shame, to be honest. We've already shown what it can do here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool, nothing magic, and it's already paying its way on our farm. Hard work and good stockmanship still matter most. Use what works and leave the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little disappointed. I'd planned my career around being the man who knows the tech and the cows. If it stalls, I'm just a good herd manager, which isn't bad, but it's not what I'd hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Squeeze more out of the robots and the herd data, and try to get our yields up another five percent. Hannah and I would keep saving for a house deposit, and maybe start trying for a baby in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet night with no alarms from the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hoped for more. More what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More responsibility, really. I'd hoped to manage a few farms' robot systems one day, not just ours. If AI stalls, there's less call for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the basics still matter. Feet, fresh cows, clean water. I tell them that anyway, but I'd tell them louder.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool, nothing magic, and it's already paying its way on our farm. Hard work and good stockmanship still matter most.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, because I planned my career around being the man who knows the tech and the cows. If it stalls, I'm just a good herd manager.
S0.do: Keeps going and pushes herd yields up about five percent using the robots and data. Saves with Hannah for a house deposit and plans to start trying for a baby in a year or two.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small disappointment about a career he'd hoped for.
S0.quote: If it stalls, I'm just a good herd manager, which isn't bad, but it's not what I'd hoped.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth already works with robots daily, so the plateau feels like a ceiling rather than relief. His traditional values show in his emphasis on hard work and basics for the apprentices. He links career plans and family plans closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I think is coming. We're half in it already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that adapt will do fine, and the government should get out of the way and let them. Less red tape, more apprenticeships. That's what I'd say at the dairy meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do very well. Every dairy around here will want someone who knows the robots and the cows. I'd be busy for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Morgans for a pay rise or a share of the profits, because I'd have offers from other farms. I'd start helping other farms set up their systems at weekends, for a fee. And I'd put some savings into a small share in a robot service company a friend is starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit worried for my apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why worried for the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because some of the jobs I'm training them for might not be there. Feeding, scraping, moving cows, robots can do more of that each year. I'd make sure they learn the systems too, not just the shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Brookside if you got a better offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'd talk to the Morgans first. They gave me this job at 24 when no one else would. Loyalty matters, but so does a fair wage.

S1.say: I'd say farms that adapt will do fine, and the government should get out of the way. Less red tape and more apprenticeships.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do very well, because every dairy nearby will want someone who knows both robots and cows. I'd be busy for years.
S1.do: Asks his employers for a pay rise or profit share, starts paid weekend work setting up systems on other farms, and invests some savings in a friend's robot service company. Makes sure his apprentices learn the systems as well as the manual jobs.
S1.feel: Excited, with some worry for his apprentices.
S1.quote: I'd make sure they learn the systems too, not just the shovel.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth sees Steady Disruption as his moment and wants government to step back. He balances ambition with loyalty to the family that hired him young. His concern for apprentices fits his belief in learning on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families, churches and communities need to look after people, because the government won't move fast enough. Work gives people dignity, so find ways to keep people doing something useful. I'd say it at church and to the young lads in the youth group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for a year or so, setting systems up. After that, if AGI can manage a herd, the Morgans don't need me. My edge would last about as long as it took to install the thing that replaced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast: offer my services to every dairy in the county in the first six months, and charge properly. I'd save every penny, no house purchase, no new car. Hannah and I would put off trying for a baby until we knew where we stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, but with a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said put off a baby. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, to be honest. Hannah's ready and so am I. But bringing a child into two years of chaos, with neither of us sure of a job, I'd want to wait. We'd pray about it, and talk, and probably wait a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the lads in the youth group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. Lads of 16 with no apprenticeship to go to, no work in two years. I'd worry about drink and trouble. I'd want the church to keep them busy, even if it's just fixing the hall roof.

S2.say: I'd say families, churches and communities need to look after people because the government won't move fast enough. Work gives people dignity, so keep people doing something useful.
S2.think: Privately I'd be fine for a year or so, setting systems up. After that, my edge would last about as long as it took to install the thing that replaced me.
S2.do: Offers his set-up services to every dairy in the county in the first six months and charges properly. Saves everything, drops plans for a house and car, and delays trying for a baby while leaning on church to keep local teenagers busy.
S2.feel: Anxious and busy, with a knot in his stomach and sadness about delaying a family.
S2.quote: My edge would last about as long as it took to install the thing that replaced me.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture, Gareth's skills buy him a short head start, and he's clear-eyed about that. His deepest worry is for teenagers in his youth group losing the path into work. Faith and family shape his response, including the hard choice to delay a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for farmers to take charge of this themselves, not wait for handouts. Buy the robots, train the young ones, own the future. I'd say that at the dairy meeting and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is my best chance to make real money. I could build a business, buy a share in a farm, and be an owner by the time AGI lands. That's how you stay safe, you own the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd set up a small company servicing dairy robots with my friend, and keep working for the Morgans part-time. By year two I'd ask the Morgans about buying a small share of the herd. I'd put two months of savings into the company and keep two back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'own the machines'. Would that sit right with your values?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Owning and working hard isn't wrong. But I'd want to employ local lads as long as I could, not just run it all off a laptop. That's where my faith comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hannah think about the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say go for it, but don't lose the house money. She's the careful one. We'd agree a limit, two months' savings and no more, and I'd stick to it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time for farmers to take charge of this themselves, not wait for handouts. Buy the robots, train the young ones and own the future.
S3.think: Privately five years is my best chance to make real money and become an owner before AGI lands. That's how you stay safe: you own the machines.
S3.do: Sets up a dairy robot service company with a friend in year one while working part-time for his employers. Asks about buying a small share of the herd in year two, and invests two months of savings while keeping two back.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more excited than scared.
S3.quote: That's how you stay safe, you own the machines.
S3.fieldNote: Gareth's free-market outlook and adaptability combine into a clear plan: own the machines before they arrive. He squares ownership with his faith by wanting to keep employing local young people. His wife sets the limit on risk, and he accepts it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a good runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people get on with it. Apprenticeships now, family farms investing now, and less paperwork. Nobody should be waiting for someone else to save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd come out of it well. By 37 I could own part of a dairy, run a service business and have a family. If AGI does the work then, at least we'd own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd stay at Brookside and do the robot service work on the side. Around year three I'd buy into the herd, and Hannah and I would buy a house and start a family. By year six or seven I'd have the service company running with three or four staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful. A bit nervous about what the world looks like at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change anything about your faith or community role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me plan for the lads in the youth group properly. I'd want the church and the young farmers' club to run apprenticeships with local farms, so they learn the robots and the cows. Ten years is time enough to get a whole group of them through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd overstretch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I like taking on too much. Hannah keeps me honest. We'd agree a plan and look at it every year at harvest, like we do the farm accounts.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people get on with it: apprenticeships now, family farms investing now, and less paperwork. Nobody should wait for someone else to save them.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd come out well, owning part of a dairy, running a service business and raising a family by 37. If AGI does the work then, at least we'd own something.
S4.do: Stays at Brookside for two years while running robot servicing on the side. Buys into the herd and a house and starts a family around year three, grows the service company to three or four staff, and sets up apprenticeships for local teenagers through church and the young farmers' club.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, a little nervous about the end point.
S4.quote: Ten years is time enough to get a whole group of them through.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Gareth build everything he wants: ownership, a business, a family, and apprenticeships for local teenagers. His drive is tempered by his wife's caution and a yearly review. The young people in his youth group are the thread through all three AGI scenarios.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not for me so much as for the lads in the youth group and my apprentices. They'd have no way in. What would help is apprenticeships that teach both the robots and the animals, and less red tape so family farms can invest and take people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Even with all the robots, a cow still needs someone who cares if she's lame. I hope whatever comes keeps a bit of that.

headlineQuote: My edge would last about as long as it took to install the thing that replaced me.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old herd manager on a 420-cow dairy that already milks with robots, married to Hannah, a vet nurse, and active in his church youth group. He's traditional and free-market, wants less red tape and more apprenticeships, and dislikes waiting for government help. He uses AI daily and sees most scenarios as a chance to own machines and part of a farm before AGI arrives. His worry in every fast picture is for the teenagers and apprentices with no route into work, and his plans for children move with the warning time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, mainly for the teenagers in his youth group and his apprentices, who would have no way into work.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships that teach both robots and animals, and less red tape so family farms can invest and take people on.
